common_name: Mercado Amaranth (Traditional Mexican Market Grain Amaranth)

planting.note: Wait until soil is thoroughly warm and frost risk has passed, since this is a late, long-season type that needs the full summer to fill its seed heads.

directions: Surface-sow seed in warm soil after frost danger has fully passed, pressing it in rather than burying it, since this variety is slow to finish and benefits from the longest possible season. Mercado grows into a tall, lodge-resistant plant topped with apple-green, cockscomb-shaped seed heads that mature to a tan, protein-rich grain prized for popping and milling. Thin seedlings to allow sturdy stems to develop, and let plants stand in full sun with only occasional watering once established. Harvest when seed heads feel dry and papery and seed threshes free with light rubbing.

common_name: Opopeo Amaranth (Michoacan Dual-Purpose Grain and Leaf Amaranth)

planting.note: Direct sow on the soil surface after the last frost, since seed needs warmth and light to germinate quickly.

directions: Scatter seed thinly over warm, prepared soil and press it in without burying it deeply, as germination is fast once temperatures climb. Opopeo is a traditional Mexican landrace named for a town in Michoacan, grown both for its tender young leaves, which can be harvested repeatedly through the season, and for its abundant cream-colored grain borne on deep magenta seed heads. Allow top growth to slow and seed heads to dry and bronze before harvesting for grain, threshing and winnowing by hand. It tolerates poor soil and drought well once rooted in, making it a reliable dual-purpose crop for hot gardens.

common_name: Oscar Blanco Amaranth (Bolivian Giant Drooping Grain Amaranth)

planting.note: Direct sow lightly and keep soil evenly moist until seedlings establish, giving this towering variety the longest possible warm season.

directions: Sow seed shallowly once soil has warmed and thin seedlings at the two-to-four-leaf stage to give this exceptionally tall heirloom room to develop its sturdy stalks. Oscar Blanco, an old Bolivian grain type, produces long, drooping, beige-to-pink tasseled seed heads reminiscent of foxtail amaranths, reaching well over ten feet in good conditions. Support plants against wind if grown in an exposed site, since the heavy, pendant seed heads can be top-heavy on tall stems. Harvest the panicles once they feel dry and papery, then thresh by rubbing or beating the heads over a cloth to collect the grain.

common_name: Aurelia's Verde Amaranth (Green-Headed Guatemalan Grain Amaranth)

planting.note: Direct sow at a shallow depth in warm, well-drained soil once frost danger has passed.

directions: Sow seed about an eighth of an inch deep in warm soil after the last frost, keeping the bed evenly moist until seedlings are established. Aurelia's Verde produces thick, sturdy stalks topped with large, pale green seed heads that yield a generous grain harvest, and it holds up well in heat with only occasional weeding and watering. Let seed heads dry fully on the plant, turning papery and lightweight, before cutting and threshing for grain. Like most grain amaranths it tolerates drought and average soil once established, making it a low-input choice for a dedicated grain bed.

common_name: Juana's Orange Amaranth (Guatemalan Maya Heirloom Grain Amaranth)

planting.note: Surface sow with minimal covering after the soil has warmed, since seed needs light and warmth to germinate reliably.

directions: Scatter seed over warm soil and press it in rather than burying it, thinning seedlings once they reach a few inches tall to give stalks room to thicken. This heirloom was revived by Maya communities in Baja Verapaz, Guatemala, and produces vivid orange-bronze seed heads atop vigorous plants grown for both nutritious grain and edible leaves. It tolerates poor soil and dry spells well once rooted, needing little more than full sun and occasional watering to thrive. Harvest seed heads as they dry and lighten in color, then thresh and winnow to collect the grain.
